items.title: Day 3 Overview — Tasks & Competencies
items.body:
Day 3 · Chapter 3: People

Day 3 Overview

Today you'll turn one-off email addresses into a real, searchable contacts list — and learn to message a whole group at once instead of typing everyone's address every time.

Competencies Covered Today

  • Use the People views
  • Work with contacts
  • Use contact groups

Today's Tasks

  1. Watch the Chapter 3 Presentation
  2. Managing People in Outlook — read, then complete Hands-On OU3-D1
  3. Contacts — read, then complete Hands-On OU3-D2–D5
  4. Contact Groups — read, then complete Hands-On OU3-D6–D8
  5. Chapter 3 Quiz (self-assessment, via eLab and Canvas)
  6. Chapter 3 Test (via eLab and Canvas)
How Hands-On grading works today

Unlike Chapter 2, today's work produces things you can screenshot directly — a saved contact, a pinned Contact Card, a contact group — so every Hands-On assignment today is graded by screenshot upload, the same as Chapter 1. Two of the exercises ask you to actually send a message (to a contact, and to a group); for those, a screenshot of the message sitting in your Sent Items folder is your proof.

items.title: Managing People in Outlook — Reading
items.body:
Day 3 · Chapter 3 Reading

Book pages: 45-47 · Chapter 3 · CBO Objective: Use the People views

Managing People in Outlook

Outlook offers several ways to display your contacts, the people you communicate with. Outlook calls the element where you store your contacts People — the terms "contacts" and "people" are used somewhat interchangeably. You can save all your contacts in the default Contacts folder, or create separate folders for related groups (work, school, and so on). You don't have to store the same amount of information for every contact — a family member might just need an email address, while a business client might get a full company name, address, phone numbers, and email. Contacts can be edited or deleted at any time; to delete one, select it and press Delete.

The Contacts List

There are five standard ways to view your contacts — People, Business Card, Card, Phone, and List — plus the option to build your own custom view. Which one you use is a personal preference; the view options live in the Current View group on the Home and View tabs when People is selected. As your list grows, scroll through it or use the Search Contacts box to find someone.

{{img:pg 46.png|Textbook page 46 — the five standard People-element view icons: People, Business Card, Card, Phone, and List}}

Using Peek

Peek lets you check your favorite people without leaving whatever element you're currently in — hover your mouse over People on the Navigation bar and a small window pops up showing your Favorites list. (You can also peek at Calendar and Tasks the same way — but not Mail.) You can dock a peek to the right side of the Outlook window to keep it visible while you work, and search your contacts right from inside the peek.

The People Toolbar

Hover your mouse over a name in a peek (or elsewhere in Outlook) and a small toolbar pops up — depending on what information you've stored for that contact, you can quickly chat, call, schedule a meeting, or send an email right from the toolbar's icons. The "…" (more) icon opens the option to edit that contact's details.

{{img:pg 47.png|Textbook page 47 — the docked Favorites peek panel, and the People toolbar that appears when you hover over a favorite contact}}

items.title: Hands-On OU3-D1: Explore the People Views & Peek
items.description:
Book pages: 46-47 · Develop Your Skills OU3-D1

Hands-On OU3-D1: Explore the People Views & Peek

Hands-On Exercise
  1. Click People on the Navigation bar.
  2. Choose View → Change View and switch through Business Card, then Phone, then back to People view.
  3. If you don't already have any contacts, quickly create one: Home → New Contact, enter a name and email address (a classmate or your instructor works fine), then Save & Close.
  4. Right-click that contact and choose Add to Favorites.
  5. Hover your mouse pointer over the People icon on the Navigation bar to open the peek, then move your mouse up onto your favorited contact until the People toolbar (call/chat/email/… icons) appears.
What to submit

One screenshot showing the People peek with the toolbar visible over your favorited contact.

No Credit — no screenshot submitted, or it doesn't show the peek

items.title: Contacts — Reading
items.body:
Day 3 · Chapter 3 Reading

Book pages: 48-54 · Chapter 3 · CBO Objective: Work with contacts

Contacts

When you create a contact, Outlook stores it in the Contacts folder of your data file. Addressing messages by selecting someone from People is faster than typing their address, and it keeps their phone number and mailing address in the same place too. The default storage format is Last Name, First Name — which is what lets you sort by either first or last name.

Creating a Contact

You create a contact in the Contact window and fill in as much (or as little) information as you want — the more you enter, the more useful your peeks and People views become later. Contacts can only be added one at a time.

{{img:pg 49.png|Textbook page 49 — the Contact window filled in with a sample contact's Full Name, Company, Job Title, Email, Display As, and Phone fields}}

Turning an Email Sender into a Contact

Another way to add someone: right-click their email address in the header of a message they sent you, and choose Add to Outlook Contacts. A contact window opens automatically so you can fill in more details.

Making a Contact a Favorite

Right-click a contact and choose Add to Favorites to make them show up in your People peek. To remove someone from Favorites, you have to dock the peek first — right-clicking a favorite from an undocked (floating) peek won't show the Remove from Favorites option at all.

Editing Contacts

To edit someone, find them (scroll, or use the Search People / Search Contacts box, which filters as you type) and open their contact window. In People, Business Card, or Card view, you can also click a letter along the left edge of the list to jump straight to contacts starting with that letter.

Contact Cards

A Contact Card shows a compact snapshot of everything you know about someone, without the empty fields you'd see in the full Contact window. Click the pin icon on a Contact Card to keep it open in its own window for reference while you work.

Sorting the Contacts List

By default the list sorts alphabetically by last name, but you can change that — for example, sort by company if you deal with a lot of different businesses. In Phone or List view, click a column header to sort by it (click again to reverse); Outlook remembers your sort order even after you close and reopen the program. You can also drag column headers to reorder them, drag the line between two headers to resize a column, and choose which columns display.

{{img:pg 52.png|Textbook page 52 — the Phone-view contact list with columns rearranged and sorted by the File As column}}

Sending Messages to Contacts

Typing an email address by hand risks typos, and remembering everyone's address gets harder as your list grows. Once someone's in your Contacts, open a new message and click To, Cc, or Bcc to pick them from the list — or just start typing their name and choose them from the suggestions. In People view, click the envelope icon below a contact's name in the Reading pane to email them directly; in every other view, select the contact and choose Email from the Ribbon.

items.title: Hands-On OU3-D2–D5: Add, Edit, Sort & Message Contacts
items.description:
Book pages: 48-54 · Develop Your Skills OU3-D2 through OU3-D5

Hands-On OU3-D2–D5: Add, Edit, Sort & Message Contacts

Hands-On Exercise

Part 1 — OU3-D2: Add New Contacts

  1. Choose Home → New Contact. Fill in a Full Name, Company (optional), Job Title, Email, and at least one phone number, then Save & Close.
  2. Open an email in your Inbox from a classmate or your instructor. Right-click their name in the message header and choose Add to Outlook Contacts. Add a phone number, then Save & Close.
  3. Go to People, right-click one of your new contacts, and choose Add to Favorites.

Part 2 — OU3-D3: Edit a Contact & Pin the Contact Card

  1. Double-click one of your contacts to open it.
  2. Edit the Company and Job Title fields, then Save & Close.
  3. Peek at People (or open the Contact Card another way) and click the pin icon at the top of the Contact Card so it stays open in its own window.

Part 3 — OU3-D4: Sort & Rearrange Columns

  1. Switch People to Phone view.
  2. Drag a column header (e.g. Business Phone) to a new position in the row.
  3. Drag the line between two column headers to resize a column.
  4. Click the Full Name column header to sort the list; click it again to reverse the sort order.

Part 4 — OU3-D5: Send a Message from Contacts

  1. In People view, click the envelope icon below one of your contacts' names in the Reading pane (or select a contact in another view and choose Email from the Ribbon).
  2. Subject: "[Your Name] — OU3-D5."
  3. Write a short message, then send it.
What to submit

Four screenshots: (1) your Contacts list showing the new contact(s) from Part 1; (2) the pinned Contact Card from Part 2; (3) the Phone-view list with rearranged/sorted columns from Part 3; (4) your Sent Items folder showing the OU3-D5 message from Part 4.

items.title: Contact Groups — Reading
items.body:
Day 3 · Chapter 3 Reading

Book pages: 55-59 · Chapter 3 · CBO Objective: Use contact groups

Contact Groups

A contact group (formerly called a distribution list) lets you send one message to the same set of people over and over without re-typing every address — useful for a project team or a client list. Once created, a group's name appears alphabetically right alongside your individual contacts in the address book; address a message to the group the same way you would an individual contact. Everyone in the group still appears individually in your address book too, so you can still email them one at a time whenever you want.

Tip: a contact can belong to more than one group.

Creating a Contact Group

A new group starts as a blank Contact Group window where you name the group and add members. Contact groups can only include people already in your People element — so to add someone new, you either add them as a contact first, or add them as a contact while you're building the group.

Note: a contact group you create for a web-based account like Outlook.com or Gmail won't be available when you access that email through a browser instead of Outlook.

{{img:pg 55.png|Textbook page 55 — the Contact Group window, named "Budget Team," with three members added}}

Sending Messages to Groups

Type the group's name into the To field the same way you would a person's name, and choose it from the suggestions. Or, with the group selected in the People list, click the Mail icon to open a new message with the group name already filled in.

Revising a Contact Group

Remove one member with Delete or the Remove Member command; delete the whole group with Delete Group — neither action can be undone. Removing someone from a group doesn't delete them from your address book, and editing a group member's information updates the real address book entry automatically. Add members at any time via Add Members, the same way you did when the group was created.

{{img:pg 57.png|Textbook page 57 — the Contact Group ribbon, calling out the Delete Group command (deletes the whole group) versus the Remove Member command (removes one member)}}

You can also drag a contact group directly into an open message — Outlook attaches it as an Outlook item the recipient can add to their own contacts. Or click Forward Group to email the group's member details directly.

items.title: Hands-On OU3-D6–D8: Create, Message & Revise a Contact Group
items.description:
Book pages: 55-59 · Develop Your Skills OU3-D6 through OU3-D8

Hands-On OU3-D6–D8: Create, Message & Revise a Contact Group

Hands-On Exercise

Part 1 — OU3-D6: Create a Contact Group

  1. Choose Home → New Contact drop-down arrow → Contact Group.
  2. Name it (e.g. "Study Group" or "Class Team").
  3. Click Add Members → From Outlook Contacts, then select 2-3 of your existing contacts (Ctrl+click to select more than one), and click OK.
  4. Save & Close.

Part 2 — OU3-D7: Send a Message to the Group

  1. Choose Home → New Email.
  2. Type the group's name in the To field and choose it from the suggestions.
  3. Subject: "[Your Name] — OU3-D7."
  4. Write a short message to the group, then send it.

Part 3 — OU3-D8: Add a New Member Who Isn't a Contact Yet

  1. Open your contact group and click Add Members → New E-mail Contact.
  2. Type a display name and email address for someone not already in your Contacts (make one up, or use a classmate you haven't added yet).
  3. Make sure Add to Contacts is checked, then click OK.
  4. Save & Close.
What to submit

Three screenshots: (1) the Contact Group window from Part 1, showing its name and members; (2) your Sent Items folder showing the OU3-D7 group message; (3) the group's membership after Part 3, showing the new member you added.
